processing: The stems are dried; in Japan the young green stems are dried and then roasted for sugina-cha.
harvest_season: Young green stems are the part used in Japan; little is documented about a set season elsewhere.
appearance_dry: Short, jointed, thin green stem pieces, browner when roasted.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green, typical of a dried-stem infusion; deeper when made from roasted stems.
taste_profile: Little is documented about its taste; expect a plain, green herbal cup, as with other dried-stem infusions, with some toastiness in the roasted Japanese form.

brewing.notes: Western-style infusion. One published guide gives about 2 to 3 g per cup, steeped 5 to 10 minutes, for no more than a week without medical supervision. Not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 12 or people with kidney disease.

vintage_note: Sold as a dried herb with no vintage: as cut herb in health shops, and as roasted sugina-cha in Japan. There is no harvest-year culture to follow. Buy from a seller who names the species, since toxic relatives such as marsh horsetail exist.
description:
Horsetail tea is an infusion of the stems of field horsetail, Equisetum arvense, a primitive flowerless plant. Spanish speakers call it cola de caballo, and Japan has its own version, sugina-cha, one of its many non-tea health teas.

It is made by drying the stems, and the Japanese style roasts the young green ones as well. That roasting is the one real choice in how it is made, and it should give a warmer cup than the plain dried herb, as roasting does with other herbal teas.

Little is documented about the taste as such, and few drink it for pleasure. Treat it as a mild green herbal infusion and keep the portion small. Most interest in it comes from folk medicine, where it has long been used as a diuretic and against bleeding.

This is one to treat with some care. The plant carries thiaminase, which breaks down vitamin B1, and steeping is reported to reduce it without removing it. Keep to short periods, and see a doctor first if you take diuretics. Always buy the named species.
history:
Folk medicine gave horsetail a strong reputation, mainly for stopping bleeding and for kidney and bladder complaints, and its long list of Spanish folk names shows how familiar it was. In Japan the roasted stems are classed among the health teas made without tea leaf.

Little is documented about the Peruvian use of this tea in particular, or about when it became a commercial product.
